title: Tao close
hookLine: eighty-one chapters, read one a day: which one will you keep?

cards: Eighty-one chapters, one a day. Some were a single picture: a wheel, a bowl, a valley. Some were advice for kings that turned out to fit a kitchen.
A few were hard, and the path said so. Now the book is shut, and the honest question is the one you'd ask after any long trip: what came home with you? Not everything.
A trip leaves most of itself behind. Today is for choosing the one chapter you'll keep in your pocket, and for one more look at the image the book keeps coming back to.

teach.h: THE BOOK THAT CAN'T BE TOLD.
teach.b: First, where it began. Tradition says an old archivist named Lao-tzu wrote it at a border gate on his way out of the country. The book itself never says who wrote it.
It opens by saying the Tao that can be told is not the lasting Tao, and then spends eighty chapters pointing anyway. Second, the empty places.
Thirty spokes around a hub, and the wheel works because of the hole in the middle. A bowl is useful for its hollow. The valley spirit never dies.
Again and again, the book sends you to look at what isn't there.
Third, the low places. Rivers and seas lead the valleys because they lie lower. The good warrior serves below.
A foot back instead of an inch forward.
Fourth, the image under all of it: water.
Chapter eight says the highest good is like water. It benefits everything, doesn't contend, and settles in the places people look down on.
Near the end, chapter seventy-eight says nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water, and yet nothing does better against the hard and strong.
Plain silk, uncarved wood, the infant's soft bones, the small village, the last words about acting without fighting: all water in different clothes.
At work, water is the person in the meeting who doesn't push, and still the conversation keeps finding its way back to them.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching keep one chapter close rather than the whole book; chapter eight, where the highest good is like water, gives the book one of its steadiest images.

o: the end of the book, and the water image running through it

games.q: you've finished all eighty-one chapters. what does today's practice ask you to do with them?
o: pick one chapter to keep, and hold it lightly.
start again at chapter one tomorrow.
games.why: a long trip leaves most of itself behind. the practice is to let one picture catch, the way a leaf catches on a stone, and keep that.

practice: Let the book's pictures pass slowly, without grabbing: a wheel's empty hub, muddy water going clear when it's left alone, a whirlwind that doesn't last all morning, a small fish cooked without poking, a thousand-mile journey starting under your feet, coarse cloth with jade inside.
One of them will catch, the way a leaf catches on a stone. Let that one be yours, and hold it lightly.

wordCard.voice: Tao close. The end of eighty-one chapters, and the image that runs through them: water, soft and low, that benefits everything and doesn't fight. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: like water. Tomorrow, a new book: a man, a tower, and a stack of attempts. Go gently.
